additional_open_research_occurrences.topic: Unrestricted reverse inclusion from zero-obstacle equality to all-obstacle equality
additional_open_research_occurrences.exact_source_line: The inclusion $\mathcal G^{\mathrm{all}}_\omega\subseteq\mathcal G_\omega$ follows by taking $F=0$. For $q=P_\omega[u]_{\mathcal I}$, \cref{prop:ideal-obstacle-reprojection} reduces the reverse inclusion to $P_{\omega,F}[u]=P_{\omega,F}[q]$ for every $F$. Membership in $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\omega,q)$ suffices. Under bounded mass and positive lower volume of $q$, this membership is equivalent to zero-obstacle equality, by \cref{prop:conditional-i-characterization}. On curves the two closure sets coincide even at zero mass, by \cref{prop:curve-all-obstacle-topology}. The relative-divisor reduction below gives higher-dimensional zero-volume cases over curves. A separate example has a base potential in the required relative envelope class and an ambient background with unbounded mass. The unrestricted implication remains unresolved here. Although $\tau^{\mathrm{all}}_\omega$ removes the fixed-obstacle gauge dependence, it still has incomplete curve families and remains strictly weaker than polar total variation on ordinary curve models, by \cref{prop:curve-all-obstacle-incomplete}.

additional_open_research_occurrences.topic: Complete topology with analytic closure and background compatibility
additional_open_research_occurrences.exact_source_line: Changing the curve areas rescales the polar distances, and a zero area removes its metric coordinate. The comparisons in \cref{prop:weighted-product-metric-comparison} quantify this change even when the active coordinates differ. If the curve backgrounds converge uniformly to zero-area forms, the diameters vanish and the potentials converge in $L^1$, uniformly over the model tuples. Their limit still contains the normalized smooth potentials of the limiting backgrounds, by \cref{cor:arbitrary-product-zero-area-collapse}. Thus these loci describe concrete degenerations beyond the positive-volume theory. Extending the complete topology to general ordinary models, while retaining analytic closure and compatibility across backgrounds, remains open.
